title: The Wizard, The Cat, and The Sky's Tantrum
markdown:
Imagine a land perched so high its valleys tickled the very clouds. Crystal-clear streams tumbled down like giggling waterfalls, and wind-whipped fir trees, with their branches reaching like eager hands, stood guard. This was wizard Merrit’s magnificent home. Merrit was clever, sure, but his real gift was preparedness. He packed enough enchanted marmalade to last a fortnight and could brew tea in a dizzying seventy-three ways. His shadow, his constant companion, was a cat named Ink. Ink was like a piece of the night itself, sleek and black, with eyes like polished obsidian, a purr that tasted of hearth-warmth, and fur that smelled faintly of rain on slate. She did not do many tricks, but her purrs were a perfect guide to Merrit’s mood, and her quiet judgements were usually spot on. Merrit always made sure Ink had the softest cushions and the tastiest fishy treats.

“A happy cat,” he would often say, “means a happy home, and a happy home is the best magic of all.”

The pact was simple, and Ink enforced it with a look: if Merrit packed the treats, Ink would come. The taboo was simpler still, though he had not yet named it. Do not yank at the sky. Do not force a flower. Do not brew seventy-three teas at a tantrum.

One blustery morning, a flustered Gilda Grub bustled up Merrit’s winding garden path. Gilda was famous for her prize-winning pumpkins and her rather oomph-y cackle. Her apron was smudged with soil. “Merrit,” she puffed, her voice creaking like an old unoiled gate. “My Glimmering Gillywort. It has vanished. Poof. Gone. And the valley’s Glow-a-thon is tomorrow. My pumpkins will be dull as dishwater without it.” Glimmering Gillywort was a special herb that shimmered under the moon, and it was key to Gilda’s glowing pumpkins. Without it, the Glow-a-thon would be a bit of a damp squib.

Merrit, ever the helpful sort, started packing straight away. He crammed in a spare cloak, three kinds of biscuits — oatmeal raisin, honey crunch, and ginger snap — and a pocket-sized telescope, just in case any rare sky-jellies decided to drift by. Ink yawned, stretched with a shimmery ripple of black fur, and with a decisive flick of her tail hopped into Merrit’s satchel. A silent agreement: she was coming along for this important mission.

The first impossible task was the weather itself. Their quest began as a gentle ramble through meadows sprinkled with buttercups, like scattered gold coins. The air smelled like fresh grass and distant pine. Merrit hummed his favourite tune, the one about the dancing dust bunnies. But as they climbed higher, following the twisty goat paths, the air began to perform. The wind, which had been a playful whisper, suddenly roared like a grumpy giant stamping its feet. Then the clouds gathered. Not fluffy cotton-ball clouds, but dramatic swirling shapes of bruised purple and angry grey. They looked like grumpy thunder-elephants marching across the sky.

“Oh, my stars and garters,” Merrit exclaimed, his spectacles nearly tumbling off his nose. “This is rather theatrical. Quite the grand entrance for a bit of weather.” Ink, usually as calm as a teacup on a steady shelf, flattened her ears and let out a tiny worried mrrrow. Suddenly buckets of rain poured down, each drop as big as a dewdrop. The world became a grey blur. Then, just as quickly, the sun burst through, painting everything in dazzling gold. Everything sparkled.

“Remarkable,” Merrit murmured, pulling out a tiny silk umbrella he had packed, just in case. “Almost as if the sky has stage fright, putting on a show and then getting shy.”

The second impossible task was to find sense in the howl. The wind carried a strange melodic whistle, like a lonely flute player in the clouds. Pine shadows striped across the mountain path. Merrit, guided by Ink’s twitching tail, found not just a sheltered mossy nook, but a small tidy cottage tucked away from the blustering wind. It looked as if it had grown right out of the hillside. Outside, a beautifully painted wooden sign read: Willow Whisper. Neatest handwriting this side of the Whispering Peaks. Inside, a woman sat at a perfectly organised desk, her quill scratching away with exquisite precision.

“Good day,” Merrit said, shaking water from his hat. “We seem to have encountered some rather enthusiastic weather on our journey.”

Willow, without looking up, finished a sentence with a delicate flourish. “Indeed, wizard,” she replied, her voice as calm and clear as a mountain spring. “The strange weather is most peculiar. I have been charting it. Each bout is more dramatic than the last. It is as if the clouds are throwing a tantrum, or perhaps having a theatrical rehearsal.”

Willow had been cataloguing the weather’s theatrics with meticulous detail. Her charts, written in perfect cursive, showed a clear pattern, a sequence of dramatic shifts that were growing more intense. “The problem,” she explained, “is not meanness, but an imbalance. Something has disturbed the valley’s natural rhythm, its gentle hum. The sky is simply overreacting, like a child who has not had their nap.”

Merrit, usually so proud of his extensive spell knowledge, found himself listening intently. Ink, perched on Willow’s tidy bookshelf, let out a soft rumbling purr. It was a sound of deep contentment that seemed to settle the very air in the cottage. Willow’s neatness and Merrit’s enthusiasm, combined with Ink’s intuitive calm, began to form a plan.

The sky is only shouting, they hummed together, the Donaldson-soft refrain of the climb. The sky is only shouting. Hush it kind.

The third impossible task was to soothe without a yank. Willow revealed a dusty old book on elemental harmony, its pages filled with intricate diagrams. “The key,” she said, tapping a diagram with a slender finger, “is gentle persuasion. Not force. Think of it like coaxing a shy flower to bloom, not yanking it from the ground.” Merrit realised with a jolt that he did not need his seventy-three tea-brewing spells or his emergency marmalade stash. He needed to work with the natural world.

Following Willow’s precise instructions, Merrit gathered a handful of sun-dried mountain herbs, their scent like a summer breeze, and a vial of pure stream water that sparkled with captured sunlight. Ink, with a gentle nudge of her head against Merrit’s leg, indicated the direction of a small secluded grove where the wind’s melody was softest. Merrit and Willow stood together in the clearing, Merrit carefully scattering the fragrant herbs while Willow hummed a soft resonant tune, her perfect handwriting having revealed the exact frequency needed to soothe the restless sky. Ink, sitting serenely at their feet, seemed to absorb the swirling energy, her purr a steady comforting anchor.

Slowly the dramatic bruised clouds began to soften, their edges becoming wispy and pale. The wind subsided into a gentle sigh, and the sun shone with a steady warm glow. The sky’s tantrum was only weather wearing a mask; its true form was the valley’s old quiet rhythm, gold and ordinary and enough. Gilda Grub’s pumpkins would glow beautifully. Merrit, though he had not needed his spare cloak or his biscuits this time, felt a warmth that had nothing to do with tea. He had kept the pact with Ink, and the sky, once shouted at, had been asked instead.

A promise kept is kinder than a satchel packed. And the Glow-a-thon, when it came, shone without a single forced spark.
characters: Merrit (wizard of preparedness and marmalade), Ink (a cat like a piece of night), Willow Whisper (a witch with the neatest handwriting)
audience: children aged 11-12, amusing mountain fantasy adventure for older children
